\chapter{Numbers Eleven to Twenty}
\label{ch:hi-numbers-eleven-to-twenty}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from eleven to twenty in Hindi and spot the subtractive nineteen sitting inside the list.}

Count \hi{ग्यारह} to \hi{बीस}, then read \hi{उन्नीस} as 'one less than twenty', the same logic as Latin's ūndēvīgintī.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[u]{\hi{उ} — the same vowel, standing on its own feet}

\label{lesson:HI-S127-letter-u}



\begin{quote}
You already have the little hook that adds a \emph{u} underneath a consonant. Before the new one: which mark is it, and where does it sit?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{उ}}
\textbf{\hi{उ}} — \emph{u}.

This is the \textbf{independent vowel}. The hook you already know rides under a consonant and cannot stand alone. When a word \textbf{begins} with \emph{u}, there is no consonant to hang the hook on, so the vowel gets a full letter of its own.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a joined upper bowl and lower loop
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script: two ways to write one sound}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where the \emph{u} falls} & \textbf{how it is written} \\
\midrule
under a consonant & the hook you already have \\
at the start of a word & \textbf{\hi{उ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both say \emph{u}. Which one a word uses is settled by \textbf{what comes before it}, and nothing else. Every vowel in this script works this way, so learning the pair once tells you what to expect from all of them.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{उ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the headline junction, curve down and left around the upper bowl, then sweep back through the waist and around the lower loop without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.} The pen comes up once and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified two-stroke teaching form; everyday handwriting may divide the bowl and loop differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \hi{उ} stroke order.svg’, panels 1–2, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{उ} three times, saying \emph{u} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} whether a word starting with \emph{u} uses the hook or the full letter
  \item \emph{Look:} at \hi{उ} and say how many times the pen leaves the page
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why can the hook not open a word? (It has nothing to hang from.) What does \textbf{\hi{उ}} carry? (\emph{\textbf{u}}.) How many pen lifts? (One.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ū]{\hi{ऊ} — the same letter, holding the note longer}

\label{lesson:HI-S128-letter-uu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \textbf{\hi{उ}} — what sound does it carry, and when does a word use it instead of the hook?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ऊ}}
\textbf{\hi{ऊ}} — \emph{ū}, the long one.

The sound is the same vowel held for longer, and the letter says so: it is \textbf{\hi{उ} with one loop added on the right}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the continuous body of \textbf{\hi{उ}}
  \item a separate right-hand loop
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script: the pair, side by side}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{body} \\
\midrule
\hi{उ} & u & bowl and loop \\
\hi{ऊ} & ū & the same, plus a right loop \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Put them next to each other and the extra loop is the only difference. That is not a coincidence of shape — \textbf{the script pairs short and long vowels by building the long one out of the short one}, and you will see the same trick again.

This letter is worth having before you can use it. The Hindi for \emph{I will come} begins with a long \emph{ū} sitting where no consonant can carry it, so the whole of the future tense waits on this one loop.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ऊ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} curve down and left around the upper bowl, then sweep back through the waist and around the lower loop without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at the waist and sweep the right-hand loop up, around, and down-left
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified three-stroke teaching form; everyday handwriting may join or simplify the loops differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \hi{ऊ} stroke order.svg’, panels 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \hi{उ} and \hi{ऊ} side by side, and name the one difference
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{उ}  ·  \hi{ऊ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ऊ} three times, holding the vowel long as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of the two takes more pen lifts, and how many
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is added to \textbf{\hi{उ}} to make \textbf{\hi{ऊ}}? (One loop on the right.) What does the extra loop do to the sound? (Holds it longer.) How many pen lifts does \textbf{\hi{ऊ}} take? (Two.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{\hi{ओ} — a letter you can already draw most of}

\label{lesson:HI-S129-letter-o}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \textbf{\hi{आ}} — what does it do? Picture its shape, and keep the picture.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ओ}}
\textbf{\hi{ओ}} — \emph{o}.

Another independent vowel, for a word that \textbf{begins} with \emph{o} and has no consonant to carry the mark.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the joined upper and lower bowls of \textbf{\hi{आ}}
  \item a swept middle shoulder, an inner stem and a trailing stem
  \item \textbf{a separate arc over the top}
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script: what is new and what is not}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{what you see} \\
\midrule
\hi{आ} & the body \\
\hi{ओ} & the same body, with an arc above \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Everything below the headline you have drawn before. \textbf{The only new mark is the arc}, and it sits above the line rather than on it, so it is easy to spot and easy to miss.

This is the third time a letter has turned out to be an old one with a piece added. That is how the script is built, and it is why the alphabet gets faster rather than slower as you go.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ओ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} curve right around the upper bowl and continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and sweep the middle shoulder right
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and descend the inner stem
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and descend the trailing stem
  \item \textbf{5.} lift at the trailing stem's headline junction and sweep the upper arc upward and left
  \item \textbf{6.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 5.} The pen comes up 5 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified modern printed teaching form; traditional and everyday handwriting may divide or simplify the curves differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \hi{ओ} stroke order.svg’, panels 1–6, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \hi{आ} and \hi{ओ} side by side, and name the one mark that separates them
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{आ}  ·  \hi{ओ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ओ} three times, saying \emph{o} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} which part of \hi{ओ} sits above the headline
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is \textbf{\hi{ओ}} built on? (\textbf{\hi{आ}}.) What is added? (An arc above the line.) What have the last three letters had in common? (Each was an older letter with one piece added.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gyārah — bīs]{\hi{ग्यारह}, \hi{बीस} — genuinely irregular, and one honest exception}

\label{lesson:HI-C22-gyarah-bees}



\begin{quote}
Be honest about this one: Hindi's teens don't follow a clean, predictable pattern the way Spanish's or Latin's do. But hiding inside that irregularity is a real echo of something Latin does too.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words — Eleven to twenty}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
11 & \textbf{\hi{ग्यारह}} & \emph{gyārah} \\
12 & \textbf{\hi{बारह}} & \emph{bārah} \\
13 & \textbf{\hi{तेरह}} & \emph{terah} \\
14 & \textbf{\hi{चौदह}} & \emph{chaudah} \\
15 & \textbf{\hi{पंद्रह}} & \emph{pandrah} \\
16 & \textbf{\hi{सोलह}} & \emph{solah} \\
17 & \textbf{\hi{सत्रह}} & \emph{satrah} \\
18 & \textbf{\hi{अठारह}} & \emph{aṭhārah} \\
19 & \textbf{\hi{उन्नीस}} & \emph{unnīs} \\
20 & \textbf{\hi{बीस}} & \emph{bīs} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{The two words — Honest irregularity}
Unlike Spanish's transparent \emph{dieciséis}-\emph{diecinueve} or even the fused-but- regular \emph{once}-\emph{quince}, Hindi's 11-18 each descend from their own Sanskrit number-word (\emph{ekādaśa, dvādaśa, trayodaśa}...) through centuries of individually unpredictable erosion. Most end in \textbf{-rah}, a worn-down echo of Sanskrit's \textquotedblleft{}-daśa\textquotedblright{} (\textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}), but the erosion of each number's front half isn't predictable from the number itself — these genuinely have to be memorized one by one, the way English speakers just memorize \textquotedblleft{}eleven\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}twelve\textquotedblright{} rather than deriving them.

\subsection*{The two words — \hi{उन्नीस}}
Here's the honest exception: \textbf{\hi{उन्नीस}} (\emph{unnīs}, 19) most likely isn't simply a worn-down \textquotedblleft{}nine-ten\textquotedblright{} — it likely continues Sanskrit's \textbf{own} special, \textbf{subtractive} name for 19: \textbf{\hi{ऊनविंशति}} (\emph{ūnaviṃśati}), literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{one less than twenty}\textquotedblright{} (from \emph{ūna}, \textquotedblleft{}less, deficient,\textquotedblright{} + \emph{viṃśati}, \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{} — a later, shortened form of the fuller Vedic \emph{ekonaviṃśati}, \textquotedblleft{}one-less-twenty,\textquotedblright{} with the \emph{eka}, \textquotedblleft{}one,\textquotedblright{} eventually dropped). Sanskrit used this same \emph{ūna-}/ \emph{ekona-} (\textquotedblleft{}one-less-than\textquotedblright{}) subtractive pattern for every number ending in 9 up through 99 — 29, 49, 99, all named as \textquotedblleft{}one less than\textquotedblright{} the next round number.

This is a genuine, striking parallel to something you already met: \textbf{Latin's own ūndēvīgintī} (\textquotedblleft{}one from twenty\textquotedblright{}) for 19, from the numbers-11-20 lesson. Two completely unrelated language families — Indo-Aryan and Italic, both descended from Proto-Indo-European but separated for thousands of years — independently landed on the exact same subtractive logic for naming nineteen.

\subsection*{The two words — \hi{बीस}}
\textbf{\hi{बीस}} (\emph{bīs}, \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{}) continues Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{विंशति}} (\emph{viṃśati}, \textquotedblleft{}twenty\textquotedblright{}).

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gyārah, bārah, terah\textquotedblright{} — 11, 12, 13, each individually memorized
  \item \textquotedblleft{}unnīs\textquotedblright{} — 19, most likely \textquotedblleft{}one less than twenty\textquotedblright{} (ūnaviṃśati), echoing Latin's ūndēvīgintī
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bīs\textquotedblright{} — twenty
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do Hindi's numbers 11-18 follow a predictable pattern the way Spanish's teens do? (\textbf{No} — each is individually eroded from its own Sanskrit ancestor and must be memorized.) What does \textbf{\hi{उन्नीस}} most likely preserve from Sanskrit, and what does it mean? (Sanskrit's \textbf{subtractive} \emph{ūnaviṃśati}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{one less than twenty}.\textquotedblright{}) What Latin number from an earlier lesson uses the exact same subtractive logic? (\textbf{ūndēvīgintī}, \textquotedblleft{}one from twenty\textquotedblright{} — two unrelated language families, the same idea.)
\end{tcolorbox}
